lead: An aircraft left alone does not hold an altitude, a heading or a bank angle. It drifts with every gust and every change of thrust. A flight control system is the chain that lets a pilot, or later a computer, demand a motion and get it: a cockpit control moves, linkage carries the movement to a surface, the surface deflects into the airflow, airloads appear, and the aircraft rotates about one of its axes. The same chain runs from a Cessna 172R to an airliner; only the source of the force changes, which is the step taken in power-assisted and fully powered controls.

sections.h3: Six freedoms, three axes, three primary surfaces

blocks.text: An aircraft has six degrees of freedom: three translations (fore-aft, lateral, vertical) and three rotations. A degree of freedom is one independent way the body can move. A flight control system commands the rotations directly; translation follows from attitude and thrust.

items: Roll — rotation about the longitudinal axis, nose to tail. The ailerons move in opposite senses: the up-going aileron cuts lift on its wing and the down-going one raises it, so the aircraft banks.
Pitch — rotation about the lateral axis, wingtip to wingtip. The elevator sits on the horizontal tail; trailing edge up pushes the tail down and the nose up.
Yaw — rotation about the vertical axis. The rudder sits on the vertical tail; trailing edge left pushes the tail right and the nose left.

blocks.text: The ailerons also cause adverse yaw: the down-going aileron makes more drag and pulls the nose away from the turn. The rudder corrects it. Together the aileron, elevator and rudder are the primary flight controls.

A pilot commands a deflection, not a force. At speed a few degrees of surface produce a large moment; the linkage gearing sets how many millimetres of stick travel give one degree of surface. That ratio is the first design choice.

sections.h3: Secondary controls work on the wing or on the surface, not on the axis directly

items: Flaps: trailing-edge surfaces on the wing. Extending them raises lift and drag, so the aircraft can fly slower for take-off and landing.
Slats: leading-edge surfaces that extend to delay stall at a high angle of attack.
Spoilers: upper-surface wing panels that lift up to spoil lift and add drag. They are used for descent, as a speedbrake, and on some aircraft to help roll.

Trim tabs: small hinged tabs on a primary surface. Moving the tab changes the hinge moment, so the surface stays deflected with little or no stick force. The tab moves the surface; the surface moves the aircraft.
Throttle: not a surface, but part of the control chain because it sets thrust.

blocks.text: Some syllabi group these as auxiliary controls. Notice the difference: a primary control changes an axis of motion, while a secondary control changes the wing's lift or the surface's hinge moment.

sections.h3: The conventional chain, part by part

blocks.text: The Cessna 172R, a four-seat single-engine trainer, has fully mechanical controls: a control wheel (yoke) on a column, two rudder pedals, a throttle, a mixture control and a manual elevator trim wheel. No hydraulic boost sits between pilot and surface. Follow one demand in a light aircraft of this kind: pull the column back; a short push-pull rod turns a bell crank under the floor; two cables run aft over pulleys; a turnbuckle in each cable sets its tension; at the tail the cable pulls the elevator horn, and the elevator rotates trailing edge up about its hinge.

head: Part
Function
rows: Pilot's pitch and roll input; rotates about two axes and pushes or pulls rods
Yaw input; push one and pull the other; also steer the nosewheel on the ground
Thrust demand; a lever connected to the engine
A pivoted lever that changes the direction of rod travel
Carries push and pull along its length; stiff in tension and compression
Carries pull only, so cables run in matched pairs
Guides a cable round a corner; changes direction, not tension
Threaded barrel between two cable ends; adjusts cable tension
Sector-shaped lever that turns linear cable travel into rotation, or back
Lever arm on the surface where the linkage attaches; gives mechanical advantage
The pivot that lets the surface rotate

blocks.text: Rods and cables do the same job by different means; the chapter on push-pull rods and cables compares them.

The chain is sized by its gearing G: the stick travel per unit of surface rotation. If friction is small, the work the pilot puts in equals the work done on the surface, F × (stick travel) = H × (surface rotation), so the stick force follows directly from the hinge moment.

blocks.where: F is the stick force in N; H is the aerodynamic hinge moment in N·m; G is the gearing in metres of stick travel per radian of surface rotation (multiply mm per degree by 57.3 and divide by 1000). Small gearing (few mm per degree) makes the aircraft twitchy and the forces high; large gearing makes the response sluggish and the forces light.

figure.caption: The elevator chain of the worked example. Pulling the column back 120 mm with 60 N turns the bell crank, the up cable pulls the upper horn with 206.3 N, and the elevator rises 25°; the pilot holds a hinge moment of 16.50 N·m. The down cable goes slack but stays pre-tensioned.

spec.aria: Side view of a light aircraft elevator control: control column pivoted on the floor, a push-pull rod to a bell crank, two cables with turnbuckles over pulleys to the upper and lower arms of the elevator horn, and the elevator deflected 25 degrees trailing edge up. The gearing 4.8 mm per degree, hinge moment 16.50 newton-metres and cable force 206.3 newtons are written below.

examples.question: The elevator of a light aircraft moves 25° when the control column travels 120 mm from neutral. The elevator horn arm is 80 mm and the rod or cable pulls at right angles to it. The pilot holds the column with 60 N. Ignoring friction, find (a) the gearing in mm per degree and in m per radian, (b) the hinge moment the pilot can hold, (c) the force in the rod at the horn and the mechanical advantage of the linkage.
steps: (a) Gearing = column travel ÷ elevator angle = 120 mm ÷ 25° = 4.8 mm per degree.
(b) With no friction, F × travel = H × rotation, so H = F × G = 60 N × 0.2750 m/rad = 16.50 N·m.
(c) The horn tip moves along an arc of 80 mm × 0.4363 rad = 34.9 mm while the column moves 120 mm.
Rod force = H ÷ horn arm = 16.50 N·m ÷ 0.080 m = 206.3 N. If the rod pulled at an angle θ to the horn, only F sin θ would turn the surface.

Mechanical advantage = rod force ÷ pilot force = 206.3 ÷ 60 = 3.44. Check: it equals the travel ratio 120 mm ÷ 34.9 mm = 3.44, and the work is the same at both ends: 60 N × 120 mm = 206.3 N × 34.9 mm = 7200 N·mm.
In a steady hold the rod moment balances the aerodynamic hinge moment; the pilot must push a little harder only to accelerate the surface or to beat friction.
examples.answer: Gearing 4.8 mm per degree (0.2750 m/rad); the pilot holds a hinge moment of 16.50 N·m; the rod carries 206.3 N, a mechanical advantage of 3.44.

traps: Putting roll on the rudder. The rudder yaws the aircraft; the ailerons roll it, and they also cause adverse yaw.

Saying large gearing makes the controls heavy. F = H ÷ G: many millimetres of stick per degree give light forces and a sluggish response; few millimetres per degree give heavy forces and a twitchy one.
Mixing the axes: roll is about the longitudinal axis, pitch about the lateral axis, yaw about the vertical axis.
Using millimetres in a hinge-moment sum. Convert the horn arm to metres (80 mm = 0.080 m), so the answer is in N·m, not N·mm.
Thinking ailerons turn the aircraft directly. They bank it; the horizontal component of lift does the turning.

quiz.q: Name the three primary flight controls and the axis each rotates the aircraft about.
quiz.a: Aileron — roll, about the longitudinal axis. Elevator — pitch, about the lateral axis. Rudder — yaw, about the vertical axis.

quiz.q: Why does the down-going aileron produce adverse yaw?
quiz.a: It increases lift on its wing but also increases drag. That extra drag on the outer wing pulls the nose away from the intended turn, so the rudder or a differential aileron linkage is needed to correct it.

quiz.q: A control column moves 100 mm and the elevator moves 20°. The hinge moment is 12 N·m. Find the gearing in mm per degree and the stick force, ignoring friction.
A trim tab reduces the stick force needed to hold an elevator deflection. Does it change the aircraft's pitch attitude by itself? Explain.
quiz.a: No. The tab changes the hinge moment on the elevator, so the elevator can stay deflected with less force from the pilot or from the linkage. The elevator deflection then changes the tail lift and pitches the aircraft. The tab acts on the surface, not directly on the aircraft.
A pivoted lever in the linkage that changes the direction of rod or cable travel.

quiz.q: Why must cables run in matched pairs while a push-pull rod need not?
quiz.a: A cable can carry only a pull, so a second cable is needed to carry the return movement. A rod is stiff in both tension and compression, so one rod carries push and pull.

quiz.q: A push rod exerts 300 N on an elevator horn whose arm is 60 mm. Assume the push rod acts at right angles to the horn arm. Find the hinge moment.
quiz.a: Arm = 60 mm = 0.06 m. Hinge moment = 300 N × 0.06 m = 18 N·m.

beyond: Not for the exam. In fly-by-wire aircraft the mechanical chain survives only as a fallback, and its extent differs from type to type: the Airbus A320 family keeps a mechanical path to the rudder and to the pitch trim, while some later types have none. Search for "control loading system", "artificial feel unit" and "Cessna 172 control rigging" to see how the parts in the table are adjusted on a real aircraft. The vocabulary here (gearing, horn arm, hinge moment) returns in the powered and fly-by-wire chapters that follow.
